name: Dietmar von Aist
credit: Dietmar von Aist, miniature in the Codex Manesse (Heidelberg, Cod. Pal. germ. 848), c. 1300–1340 · Public domain (Wikimedia Commons)
bio: Dietmar von Aist, a nobleman from Aist in Upper Austria documented between 1139 and 1171, wrote some of the earliest German love lyrics, notably women’s songs such as the lady and the falcon.
Three of his songs appear here in Frank C. Nicholson’s translation, Old German Love Songs (1907), made from the minnesingers of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries.

poems.title: A Memory
poems.author: Dietmar von Aist
poems.text:
In the linden up aloft a little bird began to sing:
Loud it was beside the wood. Then up once more my heart did spring
To a spot it knew of old; I saw the roses standing there.
They call to mind full many a thought which toward a lady I do bear.

"A thousand years it seems to me since in my lover's arms I lay.
Never mine the fault that he holds aloof so many a day.
Since I saw the flowers no more, heard no more the birds in song,
Brief indeed has been my joy, and my sorrow all too long."

poems.title: Lady and Falcon
poems.author: Dietmar von Aist
poems.text:
Lonely stood a lady
And looked across the meadow,
And looked for her lover.
She saw a falcon fly above her.
"Happy falcon that thou art!
Where thou wilt, thou may'st depart.
Thou dost choose thee in the wood
Any tree thou thinkest good.
Now have I, too, done likewise:
I chose a man with these mine eyes,
Chose him out, mine own to be.
Now fair ladies grudge it me.
Why leave they not my love alone?
Of all their lovers, sure, I wished for none!"

poems.title: Parting at Morning
poems.author: Dietmar von Aist
poems.text:
"Dear love, dost thou sleep fairly?
Alas, there wakes us early
A pretty bird that flew but now
And perched aloft upon the linden-bough."

"Full softly I was sleeping,
Child, till I heard thee weeping.
Sweet must have its sorrow still;
But all thou bid'st me, sweetheart, I'll fulfil."

The lady fell a-moaning:
"Thou'lt ride and leave me lonely.
And when wilt thou come back to me?
Alas, thou takest all my joy with thee!"
